title: Inequalities: When Answers Are Ranges, Not Points

questions.question: Solve: −3x < 15.
questions.rationale: Divide both sides by −3 and flip the inequality: x > −5. Check with x = 0: −3(0) = 0 < 15. ✓

questions.question: The interval notation for x ≥ 2 together with x < 5 is:
questions.rationale: x ≥ 2 includes 2 (closed bracket), x < 5 excludes 5 (open parenthesis): [2, 5).

questions.question: Solve the double inequality: −4 ≤ 2x + 1 < 7.
questions.rationale: Subtract 1 everywhere (−5 ≤ 2x < 6), then divide by 2: −2.5 ≤ x < 3.

questions.question: For which values of x is x² − x − 6 > 0?
questions.rationale: The upward parabola has roots −2 and 3, so it is positive outside the roots and negative between them.

questions.question: A taxi charges ₹50 fixed plus ₹12 per km. With ₹200 to spend, the inequality for the number of kilometres k is:
questions.rationale: Total cost 50 + 12k must not exceed 200: 50 + 12k ≤ 200, giving k ≤ 12.5, i.e. at most 12 full km.

questions.question: |x| > a (with a > 0) is equivalent to:
questions.rationale: 'Distance from 0 exceeds a' means two tails: x < −a or x > a.

questions.question: A bottle filler must stay within 10 mL of 500 mL. The condition on volume V is:
questions.rationale: Deviation from target: |V − 500| ≤ 10, i.e. 490 ≤ V ≤ 510 mL.

questions.question: Which operation does NOT require special care with inequalities?
questions.rationale: Addition (and subtraction) never changes the direction of an inequality; multiplication/division by any negative flips it.

questions.question: In linear programming, the best (maximum profit) solution is found:
options: At the centre of the feasible region
At a corner (vertex) of the feasible region
questions.rationale: A linear objective over a polygonal feasible region attains its optimum at a vertex — the corner-point principle used in scheduling and logistics.
